course.title: HVAC: Heating, Cooling and Fresh Air
course.lead: A free, self-paced course on how homes are heated, cooled and ventilated: what each part does, how heat gets moved from where you don’t want it to where you do, how to tell when something’s wrong, what you can safely do yourself, and when to call a licensed or certified professional.
how: Start with Lesson 1 for the big picture and Lesson 2 for the physics, then go in order or jump to the system you’re curious about.
Each lesson has diagrams, a “parts and what they do” table, a short quiz and links to go deeper. Badges show the level.
Play with the interactive pieces: the refrigeration cycle, the furnace start-up, the dew point lab, the airflow model, the thermostat and the heat-loss calculator.
Use the troubleshooting finder when something seems wrong, and climb the skill ladder one rung at a time.
course.who: Written for teens and adults with no HVAC experience. It picks up where the furnace-filter and alarm guides in Being an Adult 101 leave off.
course.why: Each lesson explains the “why” as well as the “what”: why a liquid boiling at low pressure can cool a house, how a heat pump can deliver three times more heat than the electricity it uses, why humid air drips on a cold coil. Facts and numbers come from the U.S. Department of Energy, EPA and ENERGY STAR, the Consumer Product Safety Commission, the CDC, the U.S. Fire Administration, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, NIST and OpenStax physics textbooks, and every lesson lists its sources.

lessons.title: The Big Picture
lessons.short: Heat moves from hot to cold on its own; HVAC moves it where we want it. The four jobs, the house as a system, and a map of every part.
lessons.intro: Heat always flows from warmer things to colder things, all by itself. In winter it leaks out of your house; in summer it leaks in. A heating and cooling system pushes back: it adds heat or carries it away, swaps stale air for fresh, and keeps the air from getting too damp. This lesson gives you the map, and every later lesson zooms in on one part of it.

blocks.h: Heat moves from hot to cold
blocks.html:
Physicists define heat as energy that moves because of a temperature difference, and it moves on its own in one direction only: from the warmer object to the cooler one. Touch a cold window and heat leaves your hand. Set a hot pan on the counter and heat leaves the pan.

A house is in the same situation all year. On a winter night, heat flows out through the roof, walls, windows and floor, and warm air slips out through cracks while cold air leaks in. On a summer afternoon the flow reverses: hot outdoor air and sunshine push heat inside. Left alone, the house would end up close to the outdoor temperature.

A heating system adds heat as fast as the house loses it. A cooling system has the harder job: it must carry heat from the cool inside of the house to the hot outdoors, against the direction heat flows on its own. That takes work, which is why an air conditioner needs a compressor and a good share of electricity. Lesson 4 shows how it’s done.

blocks.h: Four jobs: heat, cool, ventilate, dry
blocks.html:
HVAC stands for heating, ventilation and air conditioning. In a home, that adds up to four jobs:

  • Heating. A furnace burns gas or oil to heat air, a boiler heats water, a heat pump moves heat in from outdoors, or electric resistance turns electricity straight into heat.
  • Cooling. A central air conditioner or a heat pump pumps heat from inside to outside.
  • Ventilation. Exhaust fans and fresh-air systems swap stale indoor air for outdoor air. Most heating and cooling systems don’t bring in fresh air on their own (Lesson 8).
  • Humidity control. An air conditioner pulls water out of the air as it cools. EPA suggests keeping indoor humidity below 60 percent, ideally between 30 and 50 percent, to keep mold in check.

Two more pieces tie it together. Ducts or pipes carry the heating and cooling to each room, and controls, starting with the thermostat, decide when everything runs.

blocks.h: The house is part of the system
blocks.html:
Heating and cooling use nearly half of the energy in a typical home, according to ENERGY STAR. How much of that energy is wasted depends as much on the house as on the equipment:

  • Sealing air leaks can save 10 to 20 percent on heating and cooling bills, says the Department of Energy.
  • In a typical house, about 20 to 30 percent of the air moving through the ducts is lost through leaks, holes and poorly connected ducts (ENERGY STAR).
  • A system that’s too big for the house cycles on and off too often, which wastes energy, wears out parts and, in summer, leaves the air clammy (Lesson 10).

So when a room is always cold, the answer is often a leaky duct, a missing patch of insulation or a blocked return grille, not a bigger furnace.

• Furnace and central air. A gas furnace heats. For cooling, an outdoor condensing unit is connected by refrigerant lines to a coil that sits on top of the furnace, and the furnace’s blower moves the air for both.
  • Heat pump. One outdoor unit does both jobs, paired with an indoor air handler that usually has electric heating elements for backup.
  • Boiler and radiators. Hot water or steam heats radiators, baseboards or floors. Cooling, if any, comes from a separate system such as ductless mini-splits.
  • Ductless mini-splits. An outdoor unit feeds one or more wall-mounted indoor units with no ducts at all.
  • Geothermal heat pump. Pipes buried in the ground or set in a pond trade heat with the earth, which stays at a fairly steady temperature year-round.

This course explains how HVAC systems work in general. Your equipment’s installation and owner’s manuals give the exact settings, filter sizes and procedures. Local codes, enforced by the authority having jurisdiction (usually your city or county building department), decide what needs a permit and an inspection. Refrigerant, gas and electrical work inside the equipment belongs with licensed or EPA-certified professionals.

lessons.title: Heat, Humidity and Comfort
lessons.short: Conduction, convection and radiation; BTUs, watts and tons; sensible and latent heat; relative humidity, dew point and why an air conditioner drips.
lessons.intro: Before the machines, the physics. This lesson covers the three ways heat moves, the units HVAC uses to measure it, and why the water in the air matters as much as the temperature.

blocks.html:
• Conduction is heat moving through matter that stays put, by contact. Heat conducts through a wall from the warm side to the cold side, and through the glass of a window.
  • Convection is heat carried by a moving fluid, such as air or water. Warm air rising from a radiator is natural convection. A furnace blower pushing warm air through ducts is forced convection.
  • Radiation is heat carried by infrared light and other electromagnetic waves, which need no air at all. Sunshine through a window heats the floor, and you feel chilly sitting next to a cold window even when the air is warm, because your body radiates heat toward it.

A fireplace uses all three: most of the warmth reaches you by radiation from the flames, some heat conducts into the floor, and convection carries hot air up the chimney.

blocks.h: Measuring heat: BTUs, watts and tons
blocks.html:
In the United States, heating and cooling are measured in British thermal units. One BTU is the heat needed to raise the temperature of one pound of water by 1°F, about the energy released by burning a match. Equipment is rated by how fast it moves heat, in BTU per hour (BTU/h). A furnace label might say 60,000 BTU/h.

Cooling capacity is often given in tons. One ton of cooling is 12,000 BTU per hour, or about 3.5 kilowatts. The number comes from ice: melting one ton (2,000 pounds) of ice absorbs about 287,000 BTU, and spreading that over 24 hours gives about 12,000 BTU per hour. A “3-ton” air conditioner can remove about 36,000 BTU of heat every hour.

1 ton of cooling = 12,000 BTU/h ≈ 3.52 kW
1 kW ≈ 3,412 BTU/h    1 BTU ≈ 1,055 joules
Melting ice: 334 kJ/kg ≈ 144 BTU per pound; 2,000 lb × 144 ÷ 24 h ≈ 12,000 BTU/h

blocks.html:
Heat that changes an object’s temperature is called sensible heat, because you can sense it with a thermometer. Warming air or water follows a simple rule: heat = mass × specific heat × temperature change.

Heat that changes a substance’s phase, from solid to liquid or liquid to vapor, is called latent heat. While water boils, its temperature doesn’t rise; the energy goes into pulling the molecules apart. The same energy comes back out when the vapor condenses. The amounts are large: at body temperature it takes 2,430 kilojoules to evaporate one kilogram of water (about 1,045 BTU per pound), enough to heat almost six kilograms of water from freezing to boiling.

An air conditioner handles both. It removes sensible heat when it cools the air, and latent heat when water vapor condenses on its cold coil. In a humid climate, a big share of an air conditioner’s work goes to drying the air.

sensible heat: Q = m c ΔT    latent heat: Q = m L
water: c = 4,186 J/(kg·°C); Lf = 334 kJ/kg; Lv = 2,256 kJ/kg at 100 °C, 2,430 kJ/kg at 37 °C

Air can hold only so much water vapor, and warm air can hold much more than cold air. Relative humidity compares the water vapor in the air with the most the air could hold at its temperature. At 100 percent, the air is saturated.

Cool a parcel of air without adding or removing water, and its relative humidity climbs, because the same vapor is now closer to the limit. The temperature where it reaches 100 percent is the dew point. Cool any surface below the air’s dew point and water condenses on it. That’s why a glass of ice water sweats on a humid day, why windows fog up in winter, and why a cold-water pipe can drip in a damp basement.

OpenStax works an example: air at 25°C holding 9.40 grams of water vapor per cubic meter has a relative humidity of about 41 percent, and its dew point is 10°C. Anything in that room colder than 10°C collects water.

blocks.cap: The dew point comes from the Magnus formula with the constants of Alduchov and Eskridge (Journal of Applied Meteorology, 1996): a = 17.625 and b = 243.04 °C. It matches the saturation vapor densities in OpenStax Table 13.5 to within half a percent from 0 to 40 °C. Drag on the chart, or use the sliders, to change the air.

blocks.h: Why an air conditioner dries the air
blocks.html:
The indoor coil of an air conditioner runs colder than the dew point of the air blowing across it. Water vapor condenses on the fins, giving up its latent heat, and drips into a drain pan. From there a drain line carries it outdoors, to a floor drain or to a small pump. On a muggy day a home air conditioner can pull gallons of water out of the air.

The air leaving the coil is cool and close to saturated. As it mixes with the room and warms up, its relative humidity drops, so the room ends up both cooler and drier. EPA recommends using air conditioners or dehumidifiers when needed to keep indoor humidity in check, and keeping the drip pans clean and the drain lines flowing.

Your body sheds heat by all three methods, plus the evaporation of sweat. When the air is humid, sweat evaporates more slowly, so the same temperature feels hotter. Moving air helps sweat evaporate: the Department of Energy says ceiling fans let you raise the thermostat setting about 4 degrees with no loss of comfort. Cold windows and walls pull heat from you by radiation, which is one reason a well-insulated room feels warmer at the same air temperature.

Condensation is useful on the indoor coil, where a drain is waiting for it. Anywhere else it can cause trouble: cold ducts sweating in a hot attic, water dripping from uninsulated cold pipes, and damp spots that grow mold. EPA suggests covering cold surfaces such as cold-water pipes with insulation, and acting quickly when you see condensation on windows, walls or pipes.

quiz.q: One ton of air-conditioning capacity equals:
quiz.why: 12,000 BTU per hour, about 3.5 kilowatts: the rate that melts a ton of ice in a day.

quiz.q: What is the dew point?
opts: The temperature at which water boils
The temperature at which the air, cooled without adding or removing water, reaches 100 percent relative humidity
The coldest temperature of the day
The temperature of the indoor coil
quiz.why: At the dew point the relative humidity reaches 100 percent. Any surface colder than that collects water.

quiz.q: Why does a glass of ice water sweat on a humid day?
opts: The glass’s surface is colder than the air’s dew point, so vapor condenses on it
The glass is warmer than the air
quiz.why: The cold surface cools the air touching it below its dew point, so water vapor condenses there.

quiz.q: Which kind of heat changes a substance’s phase without changing its temperature?
quiz.why: Latent heat. An air conditioner removes latent heat when water vapor condenses on its coil.

quiz.q: What indoor relative humidity does EPA call ideal?
quiz.why: EPA suggests below 60 percent, ideally 30 to 50 percent.

lessons.title: Furnaces and Boilers
lessons.short: How a gas furnace starts up and proves each safety, the heat exchanger and venting, AFUE and condensing furnaces, electric furnaces, boilers and radiant heat.
lessons.intro: A furnace heats air; a boiler heats water. A modern gas furnace runs the same careful start-up routine every time it lights, checking its own safety devices before it lets any gas flow.

blocks.h: How a furnace heats a house
blocks.html:
A forced-air furnace has two airstreams that must never mix. Inside the heat exchanger, burning gas makes hot combustion gases, which flow through the exchanger’s passages and out the vent pipe. Outside the heat exchanger, the blower pushes house air across its hot metal walls and up into the supply ducts. Cooler air returns from the rooms through return grilles and the filter, and the loop repeats.

The wall of the heat exchanger is all that separates the flame’s exhaust from the air you breathe. That’s why the Department of Energy notes that a leak in the heat exchanger can let combustion gases into the house, and why a yearly professional inspection includes it.

blocks.cap: A typical sequence for an induced-draft gas furnace with a hot-surface igniter. Timing, parts and order vary by model; the furnace’s installation manual and the wiring diagram inside its door describe yours. Pick a fault to see how a safety stops the sequence.

blocks.html:
Each time the thermostat calls for heat, a typical modern gas furnace goes through the same steps, and its control board won’t move to the next step until the last one has proved itself:

  1. Call for heat. The thermostat connects its R and W wires, sending a 24-volt signal to the furnace’s control board (Lesson 9).
  2. Inducer starts. A small draft inducer fan starts pulling air through the heat exchanger and pushing it out the vent, clearing out any leftover gases.
  3. Pressure switch proves the draft. A switch connected by a small hose senses the suction the inducer makes. It closes only if air is really moving through the vent.
  4. Ignition. A hot-surface igniter glows bright orange, or a spark igniter starts sparking.
  5. Gas valve opens. Gas flows to the burners and lights.
  6. Flame sensor proves the flame. A thin metal rod in the flame carries a tiny electric current that only a flame can complete. If the board doesn’t see that current within a few seconds, it shuts the gas valve.
  7. Blower starts. After a short delay, so the heat exchanger can warm up, the blower starts sending warm air to the rooms.
  8. Shutdown. When the room reaches the set temperature, the thermostat opens the W circuit. The gas valve closes, the inducer runs a little longer to clear the flue, and the blower runs on to pull the leftover heat out of the heat exchanger.

blocks.h: Safety switches: prove it, or no gas
blocks.html:
The pattern is the same throughout: no proof, no gas. The pressure switch must prove the vent is drawing before ignition. The flame sensor must prove a flame within seconds or the gas shuts off. A high-limit switch on the heat exchanger opens if it overheats, which usually means the blower can’t move enough air, for example because the filter is clogged; the burners shut off and the blower keeps running to cool things down. Many furnaces also have flame rollout switches near the burners that shut the gas off if flames spill out of the burner area.

When a safety trips over and over, it’s doing its job, telling you something is wrong. Many control boards blink a status light in a pattern that the furnace’s manual explains.

blocks.html:
A furnace’s efficiency is rated by its annual fuel utilization efficiency, or AFUE: the share of the fuel’s energy that becomes heat in the house over a typical year. A 90 percent AFUE furnace turns 90 percent of the fuel’s energy into heat for the home; the rest is lost up the vent and elsewhere. The Federal Trade Commission requires new furnaces and boilers to show their AFUE.

The Department of Energy describes three generations:

  • Older, low-efficiency systems with a natural draft and a continuous pilot light: 56 to 70 percent AFUE.
  • Mid-efficiency systems with an exhaust fan and electronic ignition: 80 to 83 percent.
  • High-efficiency condensing systems with a second heat exchanger and sealed combustion: 90 to 98.5 percent.

A condensing furnace cools its exhaust so much in the second heat exchanger that the water vapor from combustion condenses, giving back its latent heat (Lesson 2). The condensate is acidic, so it needs a drain, and the cool exhaust usually leaves through plastic pipe. With sealed combustion, the burner takes its air from outdoors through a pipe instead of using heated house air, which also lowers the risk of combustion gases entering the house.

Under the federal rule in 10 CFR 430.32, most new gas furnaces made since November 19, 2015 must reach at least 80 percent AFUE, and the same rule sets 95 percent for those made on or after December 18, 2028. Standards can change, so check the Department of Energy for the current ones.

AFUE = annual heat delivered to the home ÷ annual fuel energy used
Example: a 95% AFUE furnace burning gas worth $1,000 a year puts about $950 of it into heat for the house.

blocks.html: An electric furnace heats air with resistance elements, like a giant toaster. It has no flame and no vent, so nearly all of its energy becomes heat: the Department of Energy puts electric furnaces at about 95 to 100 percent AFUE. But electricity usually costs more than gas or oil for the same heat, so DOE suggests that people heating with electricity consider a heat pump instead (Lesson 6).

A boiler heats water instead of air. Hot-water systems pump the water through pipes to baseboard radiators, cast-iron radiators, tubing in the floor (radiant floor heat) or a coil in an air handler. Steam boilers send steam through pipes to radiators, where it condenses and runs back as water; they run hotter and are less efficient than hot-water systems.

A hot-water system adds a circulating pump, an expansion tank that makes room for the water as it heats and expands, and a pressure-relief valve. DOE lists the pro’s yearly checks: testing the pressure-relief valve and high-limit control on hot-water systems, and draining sediment and testing the low-water cutoff on steam boilers. Under 10 CFR 430.32, gas-fired hot-water boilers made since January 15, 2021 must reach at least 84 percent AFUE, and gas-fired steam boilers 82 percent.

• Check and change the filter on schedule (Change a Furnace Air Filter). A clogged filter is a top cause of limit-switch trips.
  • Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet away from heating equipment, as the U.S. Fire Administration advises for all heat sources.
  • Keep the furnace’s outdoor vent and air-intake pipes clear of snow and debris (USFA).
  • Install CO alarms on every level of the home and outside sleeping areas, and test them monthly (Test Smoke and CO Alarms).
  • Have the furnace or boiler professionally inspected and serviced every year, as CPSC, CDC and the U.S. Fire Administration all advise.

• If your CO alarm sounds, move everyone outside to fresh air right away and call 911 or the fire department; don’t go back in until responders say it’s safe (CPSC). Don’t run the furnace again until it has been serviced.
  • If you smell gas (a rotten-egg odor), follow your gas utility’s emergency instructions right away. A gas smell is an emergency for the utility, not a repair job.
  • Never jumper, bypass or disable a safety switch, and don’t open the burner compartment or touch the gas valve. Ignition, gas pressure and venting work belong with a qualified technician.
  • Yellow, wavering flames instead of steady blue ones mean the gas isn’t burning cleanly and an adjustment may be needed (DOE). Soot around the furnace is another sign. Have it checked.

quiz.q: What does the furnace’s pressure switch prove before ignition?
opts: That the gas pressure is high enough
That the draft inducer is really moving air through the vent
That the thermostat is calling for heat
quiz.why: It senses the suction the inducer makes, proving the vent path is open before any gas flows.

quiz.q: The burners light, but the flame sensor doesn’t detect the flame. What happens?
opts: The control board shuts the gas valve within seconds
The furnace keeps running at half power
quiz.why: No proof, no gas: without a flame signal, the board closes the gas valve, and it may try again before locking out.

quiz.q: A furnace is rated 95 percent AFUE. What does that mean?
opts: It runs 95 percent of the time
About 95 percent of the fuel’s energy becomes heat in the house over a typical year
It heats the house to 95 degrees
It uses 95 percent less gas than an old furnace
quiz.why: AFUE is the share of the fuel’s energy that becomes useful heat over a year.

quiz.q: Why does a condensing furnace need a drain?
opts: To empty the heat exchanger each spring
Its second heat exchanger condenses the water vapor in the exhaust
Gas leaves water behind in the burners
quiz.why: Cooling the exhaust condenses its water vapor, which recovers latent heat but leaves acidic water that must drain away.

quiz.q: What does a boiler heat?
quiz.why: A boiler heats water, which carries the heat to radiators, baseboards or floors.

lessons.title: The Refrigeration Cycle
lessons.short: Compressor, condenser, expansion device and evaporator: how a refrigerant boils where it’s cold, condenses where it’s hot, and carries heat uphill.
lessons.intro: Air conditioners, heat pumps, refrigerators and dehumidifiers all run the same loop. A fluid boils where it’s cold, soaking up heat; a compressor squeezes it; then it condenses where it’s warm and gives the heat away. This is the heart of the course.

blocks.h: The big idea: boil it cold, condense it hot
blocks.html:
Two facts from Lesson 2 make the whole cycle work. First, a liquid soaks up a lot of heat when it evaporates, and gives the same heat back when it condenses. Second, the temperature at which a liquid boils depends on the pressure. Water boils at 100°C at normal air pressure, but at higher pressure it stays liquid at higher temperatures, which is how a pressure cooker cooks faster.

A refrigerant is a fluid picked to boil at low temperatures. Keep it at low pressure and it boils colder than your living room, so it can soak up heat from indoor air. Squeeze it to high pressure and it condenses at a temperature hotter than the outdoor air, so it gives that heat away outside. The machine’s whole job is to keep one side of the loop at low pressure and the other at high pressure.

Press play to watch the refrigerant go around, or step through it one stage at a time. Colors show the refrigerant’s state, from cold liquid (blue) to hot gas (red). The COP readout is the Carnot limit from OpenStax: the best any machine could do between the temperatures you set. The coil temperatures use the gap you choose, an assumption of the model.

blocks.html:
1. Compressor. Takes in cool, low-pressure refrigerant vapor and squeezes it into hot, high-pressure vapor. This is where the electricity goes in.
  2. Condenser. A coil of tubing and thin fins, with a fan blowing air across it. The hot vapor gives its heat to the air and condenses into a warm, high-pressure liquid.
  3. Expansion device (also called a metering device). A small opening, such as a thermostatic expansion valve, an electronic valve or a fixed orifice, that the liquid squeezes through. On the far side the pressure drops; some of the liquid flashes into vapor, and that chills the rest. Out comes a cold mix of liquid and vapor.
  4. Evaporator. Another finned coil. Warm air blowing across it gives up heat, and the cold refrigerant boils into vapor as it absorbs that heat. The vapor flows back to the compressor, and the loop starts again.

In a central air conditioner, the evaporator is the indoor coil and the condenser is in the outdoor unit. In a heat pump running in heating mode, they trade jobs (Lesson 6).

blocks.html:
Energy is conserved, so all the heat the evaporator picks up indoors, plus all the work the compressor puts in, comes out at the condenser. That’s why the air blowing out of an outdoor unit in summer feels hotter than the outdoor air.

The efficiency of a cooling machine is its coefficient of performance (COP): the heat it removes divided by the work it uses. OpenStax notes that real air conditioners and refrigerators have COPs from about 2 to 6, so they move two to six times more heat than the electricity they use.

The second law of thermodynamics sets a ceiling, the Carnot limit, which depends only on the two temperatures in kelvins. The smaller the temperature lift, the higher the limit. Between a 75°F room (297 K) and a 95°F afternoon (308 K), no machine could beat a COP of about 27. Real machines fall far short, partly because the indoor coil must run colder than the room and the outdoor coil hotter than the outdoor air, which widens the lift. Larger coils, clean coils and good airflow keep that gap small.

COPcooling = Qc ÷ W    Qh = Qc + W
Carnot limit: COPcooling ≤ Tc ÷ (Th − Tc)  (temperatures in kelvins)
EER (BTU/h per watt) = 3.412 × COP

Refrigerants have changed as their side effects became known. R-22, an HCFC, damages the ozone layer; since January 1, 2020, no new R-22 may be made in or imported into the United States, though recycled and reclaimed R-22 remains available for existing systems. Its replacement in most new systems, R-410A, doesn’t harm the ozone layer but is a potent greenhouse gas: EPA lists its global warming potential (GWP) as 2,090. GWP compares a gas’s warming effect with the same amount of carbon dioxide, which has a GWP of 1.

New home air conditioners and heat pumps are moving to refrigerants with a GWP of 700 or less, such as R-454B (GWP 470) and R-32 (GWP 675). EPA lists both in safety class A2L and accepts them “with use conditions,” so equipment, tools and procedures are built for them. Lesson 5 covers the rules and dates.

blocks.h: Refrigerant work is for certified technicians
blocks.html: Under EPA’s Section 608 rules, a technician must be certified to attach gauges to a system, add or remove refrigerant, or do anything else that could release it. Intentionally venting refrigerant during service, repair or disposal is illegal. The refrigerant is also under high pressure and can cause frostbite-like burns. If your system is low on refrigerant, it has a leak, and EPA advises asking the technician to find and fix the leak rather than just adding more.

quiz.q: In an air conditioner, where does the refrigerant absorb heat from the house?
quiz.why: The cold refrigerant boils in the evaporator, soaking up heat from the indoor air blowing across it.

quiz.q: What does the expansion device do?
opts: Drops the pressure, so the refrigerant gets cold
quiz.why: Squeezing through a small opening drops the pressure; some liquid flashes to vapor and chills the rest.

quiz.q: Why must the compressor raise the refrigerant’s pressure?
opts: So it fits in smaller pipes
So it condenses at a temperature hotter than the outdoor air and can give its heat away there
To make it flow faster through the evaporator
quiz.why: Higher pressure means a higher condensing temperature. Heat only flows out to the air if the refrigerant is hotter than the air.

quiz.q: Compared with the heat removed from the house, the heat released outdoors is:
quiz.why: Q_h = Q_c + W: the outdoor coil dumps the indoor heat plus the energy the compressor added.

quiz.q: What happens to the Carnot limit on COP as the indoor and outdoor temperatures get farther apart?
quiz.why: A bigger temperature lift means a lower limit, which is why air conditioners work hardest on the hottest days.

lessons.title: Air Conditioners
lessons.short: Split systems, the indoor coil, the condensate drain and pan, SEER2 and EER2, and EPA’s rules on refrigerants and certification.
lessons.intro: A central air conditioner is the refrigeration loop split in two: a hot half outside, a cold half inside, joined by two copper lines. This lesson walks through both halves, the water they make, how efficiency is rated, and the rules that govern the refrigerant.

blocks.html:
Most central air conditioners in U.S. homes are split systems. The outdoor condensing unit holds the compressor, the condenser coil wrapped around its sides, and a big fan on top that pulls air through the coil and blows it upward. It also holds the electrical parts that start the compressor and fan, such as a contactor, which the thermostat’s 24-volt cooling signal switches on.

Inside, the evaporator coil usually sits on top of the furnace, or inside an air handler, in a box called the plenum. The furnace’s or air handler’s blower moves the air across it. A copper line set joins the two halves: a larger, insulated suction line and a smaller liquid line.

Other setups use the same loop. A packaged unit holds everything in one cabinet outdoors, connected to the ducts. A window or portable air conditioner is a tiny packaged unit. Ductless mini-splits are covered in Lesson 6.

blocks.html:
Because the indoor coil runs below the dew point of the air crossing it, water condenses on its fins all summer long (Lesson 2). It drips into the drain pan and flows down the condensate line. You can often find the end of that line outside near the foundation, dripping steadily on a humid day, or near a floor drain in the basement. Where gravity can’t do the job, a small condensate pump lifts the water away.

If the drain line clogs, water backs up and overflows. ENERGY STAR notes that a plugged drain can cause water damage in the house and affect indoor humidity, so a technician checks it at each tune-up. EPA advises keeping drip pans clean and drain lines unobstructed and flowing. Your system’s manual describes any drain care the manufacturer recommends.

A central air conditioner’s efficiency is rated two ways:

  • SEER2, the seasonal energy efficiency ratio: the cooling it delivers over a typical cooling season divided by the electricity it uses, in BTU per watt-hour.
  • EER2, the energy efficiency ratio: its efficiency at a single, hot peak condition, when it’s working hardest.

The “2” marks a change. On January 1, 2023, the Department of Energy began requiring a revised test procedure designed to better reflect real-world installation and use. Ratings under the new test (SEER2, EER2 and, for heat pumps, HSPF2) aren’t directly comparable to the old SEER, EER and HSPF numbers, so compare like with like. The same date brought new minimum efficiencies that depend on where you live:

head: Region
Split systems under 45,000 BTU/h
Split systems 45,000 BTU/h or more

blocks.html: In the North, the rule follows the date a unit was made: one built before 2023 to the old standard can still be installed. In the Southeast and Southwest, it follows the installation date for split systems: anything installed from January 1, 2023 on must meet the new minimums. In the Southwest, units must also meet an EER2 minimum (11.7 for smaller split systems with a SEER2 below 15.2) so they hold up on the hottest afternoons. ENERGY STAR certified models beat these minimums.

Certification. EPA’s Section 608 rules require anyone who attaches hoses and gauges to an air conditioner, adds or removes refrigerant, or otherwise opens the refrigerant circuit to be certified. There are four types: Type I for small appliances, Type II for high- and very-high-pressure equipment (which includes home central air conditioners and heat pumps), Type III for low-pressure equipment, and Universal for all of them. Technicians earn certification by passing an EPA-approved test given by an EPA-approved certifying organization, and the certification doesn’t expire. Apprentices may do the work only under the close, continual supervision of a certified technician.

No venting. It’s illegal to intentionally release refrigerant while servicing, repairing or disposing of equipment.

The R-22 phaseout. Since January 1, 2020, no new R-22 has been made in or imported into the U.S. EPA does not require homeowners to replace working R-22 systems, and recycled or reclaimed R-22 is still available for service. There are no “drop-in” replacements for R-22, and EPA doesn’t require converting old units to another refrigerant.

Lower-GWP refrigerants. Under EPA’s Technology Transitions rule, new residential and light commercial air conditioners and heat pumps must use refrigerants with a global warming potential of 700 or less. For self-contained units such as window and portable air conditioners, that applies to products made or imported from January 1, 2025. For split systems, it applies to systems installed from January 1, 2025, except systems whose components were all made or imported before that date: a May 2026 EPA rule removed the deadline for installing that older inventory. Existing systems can keep running and can be serviced and repaired for their whole useful life.

• Change or clean the filter on schedule (Change a Furnace Air Filter).
  • Keep leaves, grass clippings, plants and stored items away from the outdoor unit, following the clearances in its manual.
  • Know where your condensate line ends, and glance at it on humid days: steady dripping in summer is normal.
  • If the system won’t start, check the thermostat setting and the breakers (Reset a Tripped Circuit Breaker).
  • Schedule a cooling checkup in the spring, as ENERGY STAR suggests.

• Anything involving refrigerant: low charge, leaks, ice that keeps coming back after you’ve changed the filter. Ask for the technician’s Section 608 certification, as EPA suggests.
  • A humming outdoor unit whose fan won’t spin, or a breaker that trips again: turn the cooling off at the thermostat and call. The outdoor unit holds 240-volt circuits and parts that start motors; leave its panels closed.
  • Water overflowing from the indoor unit, especially near electrical parts.

lessons.title: Heat Pumps
lessons.short: The reversing valve, why a heat pump’s COP beats 1, HSPF2, cold-climate models, backup heat and defrost, ductless mini-splits and geothermal systems.
lessons.intro: A heat pump is an air conditioner that can run backward. In winter it pulls heat out of cold outdoor air, or out of the ground, and pumps it inside. Because it moves heat instead of making it, it can deliver several times more heat than the electricity it uses.

blocks.html:
A heat pump has the same four parts as an air conditioner (Lesson 4), plus a reversing valve near the compressor. The valve changes the direction the refrigerant flows through the rest of the loop, so the two coils trade jobs.

  • Cooling mode: the indoor coil is the evaporator, absorbing heat from the house; the outdoor coil is the condenser, dumping it outside.
  • Heating mode: liquid refrigerant in the outdoor coil absorbs heat from the outdoor air and evaporates, even when that air feels cold. The compressor squeezes the vapor, and the indoor coil becomes the condenser, releasing the heat into the air the blower sends through the house.

Cold air still holds plenty of heat. Air at freezing is about 273 kelvins above absolute zero; the refrigerant only has to be colder still to soak some of that heat up.

blocks.h: Why the COP can be more than 1
blocks.html:
For heating, a heat pump’s coefficient of performance is the heat delivered divided by the electricity used. An electric furnace or baseboard heater turns each unit of electricity into one unit of heat: a COP of 1. A heat pump delivers the electricity’s energy plus the heat it gathered outdoors, so its COP is always more than 1. OpenStax notes that real heat pumps have COPs of about 2 to 4.

The Department of Energy says an air-source heat pump can deliver up to three times more heat energy to a home than the electrical energy it uses, and can cut the electricity used for heating by about 50 percent compared with electric furnaces and baseboard heaters.

The Carnot limit shows why the outdoor temperature matters. OpenStax works an example: pumping heat from air at −15°C (258 K) into a hot coil at 45°C (318 K), the best possible COP is 318 ÷ 60 = 5.30. Each joule of electricity could then bring in 4.3 joules from the cold air. The colder it gets outside, the bigger the lift and the lower the limit.

COPheating = Qh ÷ W = 1 ÷ Eff    COPheating = COPcooling + 1
Carnot limit: COPheating ≤ Th ÷ (Th − Tc)  (kelvins)
OpenStax example: 318 K ÷ (318 K − 258 K) = 5.30

blocks.h: Cold weather, backup heat and defrost
blocks.html:
As the outdoor temperature drops, a heat pump has to lift heat farther, so its efficiency falls, and it runs longer to keep up. Heat pumps were long limited to places without extended spells below freezing, but the Department of Energy says newer designs are a real heating option in colder regions, and that cold-climate heat pumps are designed to work in temperatures as low as 5°F. DOE advises that buyers in cold climates look for the highest heating rating they can get.

Most ducted heat pumps have backup heat, usually electric resistance elements in the air handler, for the coldest hours, for defrost, and for emergencies. Many thermostats show it as “aux” or “emergency” heat. Backup heat works at a COP of 1, so a heat pump that leans on it too much costs more to run.

In cold, damp weather, frost builds up on the outdoor coil and blocks the airflow. The heat pump melts it with a defrost cycle: a defrost control can flip the reversing valve for a few minutes so hot refrigerant flows through the outdoor coil. DOE recommends models with demand-defrost controls, which defrost only when needed and so use less energy.

blocks.h: Rating a heat pump: HSPF2 and SEER2
blocks.html: A heat pump gets two seasonal ratings. SEER2 rates its cooling, as for an air conditioner. HSPF2, the heating seasonal performance factor, rates its heating: the heat it delivers over a typical heating season divided by the electricity it uses, in BTU per watt-hour. Since January 1, 2023, new split-system heat pumps must reach at least 14.3 SEER2 and 7.5 HSPF2 nationwide. DOE suggests putting more weight on SEER2 in hot climates and on HSPF2 in cold ones.

A ductless mini-split is a heat pump (or air conditioner) with no ducts. An outdoor unit connects to one or more indoor units, usually mounted high on a wall, through a bundle of refrigerant lines, wiring and a condensate drain. DOE notes that installing one takes only about a three-inch hole through the wall. Multi-zone systems can serve up to eight rooms from one outdoor unit, each with its own setting.

With no ducts, there are no duct leaks, which makes mini-splits popular for additions, older homes with radiators, and rooms the central system can’t reach. Each indoor unit has its own filter to clean and its own drain line.

A few feet below the surface, the ground stays at a fairly steady temperature all year, about 40°F to 70°F depending on where you live, says the Department of Energy. A geothermal heat pump trades heat with the ground through a loop of buried pipe, so in winter it lifts heat from ground that’s warmer than the air, and in summer it dumps heat into ground that’s cooler than the air. Smaller lifts mean higher COPs.

DOE describes four loop types: three closed loops (horizontal trenches, vertical boreholes, and pond or lake loops) and an open loop that uses well or surface water. Compared with air-source heat pumps, DOE says geothermal systems are quieter, more efficient and longer-lasting: up to 24 years for the indoor parts and 50 years or more for the ground loop. They cost several times more to install, which DOE says energy savings can repay in 5 to 10 years.

Three times more electricity than heat

lessons.title: Ducts, Airflow and Filters
lessons.short: The blower, supply and return ducts, registers and grilles, static pressure, filters and MERV ratings, duct leaks and sealing, balancing and zoning.
lessons.intro: The furnace or heat pump makes the heating and cooling; the blower and ducts deliver it. A great furnace on bad ducts still leaves rooms too hot, too cold or dusty, and wastes a good share of the energy you pay for.

blocks.html:
A forced-air system moves air in a loop. Return grilles pull room air into the return ducts. The air passes through the filter, then the blower, then across the furnace’s heat exchanger or the cooling coil. It leaves through the supply plenum, a box on top of the unit, and travels down a trunk duct that feeds smaller branch ducts. Each branch ends at a register in a room, often with adjustable louvers. Then the air finds its way back to a return grille, and the loop repeats.

Every bit of air pushed into the rooms has to come back. If a room gets plenty of supply air but has no easy way back to a return, for example when its door is closed, it can end up stuffy, and the system moves less air overall.

blocks.html: A cooling coil or heat pump needs a steady stream of air to work as designed. The Department of Energy puts it at about 400 to 500 cubic feet per minute (cfm) for each ton of capacity, so a 3-ton system moves roughly 1,200 to 1,500 cfm. Too little air hurts: ENERGY STAR says airflow problems can reduce a system’s efficiency by up to 15 percent, and poor airflow can leave the air overly damp. DOE notes that technicians can raise the airflow by cleaning the indoor coil or increasing the fan speed.

blocks.h: Static pressure: what the blower pushes against
blocks.html:
The blower makes a small pressure difference that pushes air through the filter, the coil, the ducts and the registers. Each of them resists the flow, and technicians measure the total resistance as static pressure, in inches of water column. One inch of water is about 249 pascals, about a quarter of one percent of the air pressure around you, which shows how gentle these pressures are.

Resistance adds up along the path. A clogged filter, a dirty coil, crushed flexible duct, closed registers and blocked return grilles all raise it, and the blower then moves less air. The widget below shows the effect.

blocks.cap: An illustrative model, not a measurement of any real system: pressure losses grow with the square of the airflow, and the blower pushes less air against more resistance. Real numbers depend on the blower, the ducts and the filter. The 400 to 500 cfm per ton band is from the Department of Energy.

blocks.html:
The filter protects the blower and coil from dust and cleans the air you breathe, but only while the fan is running. Filters are rated by MERV, the Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value, from a national consensus test (ASHRAE Standard 52.2) that reports values from MERV 1 to MERV 16. A higher MERV removes more of the small particles. Flat panel filters typically rate MERV 1 to 4; pleated filters typically rate MERV 5 to 13 or higher, and only MERV 13 and above must catch at least half of the smallest particles in the test (0.3 to 1 micrometer).

EPA suggests choosing at least a MERV 13 filter, or the highest-rated filter your system’s fan and filter slot can handle, and asking an HVAC technician to be sure it will work, because a denser filter can resist airflow more. It should fit snugly so air doesn’t sneak around it. EPA says manufacturers typically recommend replacing filters every 60 to 90 days; ENERGY STAR says to check the filter every month and change it at least every three months, or sooner if it looks dirty.

ENERGY STAR estimates that in a typical house, about 20 to 30 percent of the air moving through the ducts is lost through leaks, holes and poorly connected ducts. When those ducts run through an attic, crawlspace or garage, the heated or cooled air is simply lost outside the living space. Leaky return ducts can also pull in dusty or humid air from those spaces. Signs include high bills, rooms that are hard to heat or cool, and tangled or kinked flexible ducts.

ENERGY STAR says sealing ducts can improve a system’s efficiency by as much as 20 percent. It recommends sealing leaks with mastic sealant or metal tape, never cloth “duct tape,” which doesn’t last, and insulating the ducts you can reach in attics, crawlspaces, unfinished basements and garages. A contractor can test the whole system for leaks and repair the ones out of reach.

Balancing means adjusting how much air each room gets. Many branch ducts have a manual damper, a metal plate inside the duct turned by a lever on the outside, and registers have louvers. A zoned system goes further, with motorized dampers and a thermostat for each zone, so the upstairs can cool while the downstairs rests. Ductless mini-splits are zoned by design.

Keep supply registers and return grilles open and clear of furniture, rugs and curtains. Every closed or blocked opening adds resistance for the whole system, as the widget shows.

lessons.title: Ventilation and Indoor Air
lessons.short: Why homes need fresh air, exhaust fans, HRVs and ERVs, humidity targets and mold, and carbon monoxide from fuel-burning appliances.
lessons.intro: A furnace and an air conditioner mostly recirculate the same indoor air. Bringing in fresh air, getting rid of moisture and keeping combustion gases out are separate jobs, and they matter for your health.

blocks.html:
Cooking, showers, cleaning products, furniture, people and pets all add moisture and pollutants to indoor air. EPA says the most effective fix is usually to remove or reduce the sources. The next is ventilation: replacing indoor air with outdoor air.

Most home heating and cooling systems, including forced-air furnaces, don’t mechanically bring fresh air into the house, EPA notes. Older homes get theirs through open windows and doors and through leaks in the building. As homes are sealed better to save energy, those accidental leaks shrink, so newer homes add planned ventilation instead.

Bathroom and kitchen fans that exhaust to the outdoors remove moisture and pollutants right where they’re made, says EPA. Run the bathroom fan or open a window when showering, and use the kitchen fan while cooking. EPA also recommends venting clothes dryers, stoves and other appliances that produce moisture to the outside where possible. A fan that only blows into the attic moves the moisture to a place where it can cause mold.

Whole-house systems ventilate the entire home on purpose. Some simply run an exhaust fan and let fresh air leak in to replace it; others blow in filtered outdoor air. A balanced system does both at once, with matched fans.

Balanced systems often use a heat recovery ventilator (HRV), also called an air-to-air heat exchanger. Stale outgoing air and fresh incoming air pass each other through a core of thin plates without mixing, and heat moves across the plates. In winter the incoming air is warmed by the air leaving; in summer it’s cooled. An energy recovery ventilator (ERV) also transfers moisture, so it can help keep humid outdoor air from making the house damp in summer, and keep winter air from getting too dry.

blocks.html:
EPA’s rule is simple: the best way to control mold is to control moisture. It suggests keeping indoor relative humidity below 60 percent, ideally between 30 and 50 percent, which you can check with an inexpensive hygrometer. Air conditioners and dehumidifiers lower humidity; exhaust fans remove it at the source.

If you see condensation on windows, walls or pipes, EPA says to dry the surface and reduce the moisture source quickly, and to insulate cold surfaces such as cold-water pipes. Keep air conditioner drip pans clean and drain lines flowing (Lesson 5). If you suspect the heating and cooling system itself is contaminated with mold, EPA advises not running it until it’s cleaned.

Carbon monoxide (CO) is an odorless, colorless gas that kills without warning, says the CDC. Gas- and oil-burning furnaces, boilers and water heaters, along with portable generators, vehicles and charcoal grills, can produce it when they aren’t working or aren’t vented properly. The most common symptoms are headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion, often described as flu-like.

Prevention, from CDC, CPSC and the U.S. Fire Administration:

  • Have your heating system, water heater and any other gas-, oil- or coal-burning appliances serviced by a qualified technician every year.
  • Install CO alarms on every level of the home and outside sleeping areas, avoiding spots near heating vents or where furniture or drapes can cover them. CPSC recommends alarms that meet the current UL 2034 standard.
  • Test CO alarms monthly, and replace them as the manufacturer directs (CDC says every five years if no instructions are given).
  • Keep the vents for the furnace, dryer, stove and fireplace clear of snow and debris.
  • Never run a generator inside the home or garage, even with doors and windows open.

From the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission:

  • Never ignore it. Don’t try to find the source of the CO.
  • Immediately move outside to fresh air.
  • Call your emergency services, fire department or 911, then do a head count to check that everyone is out.
  • Don’t go back in until the emergency responders give you permission.
  • If the source is a malfunctioning appliance, don’t use it again until trained personnel have serviced it.

Practice the plan with your household (Test Smoke and CO Alarms).

lessons.title: Controls and Thermostats
lessons.short: The 24-volt control circuit and the letters on the wires, on-off cycles, programmable and smart thermostats, setback savings, and where a thermostat belongs.
lessons.intro: A thermostat is a switch with a thermometer attached. It doesn’t carry the power that runs the furnace or the compressor; it closes small 24-volt circuits that tell relays and control boards in the equipment what to do.

blocks.html:
Most central heating and cooling systems use a low-voltage control circuit. A small control transformer inside the furnace or air handler steps the house’s 120-volt power down to 24 volts AC. One wire, R, brings that 24 volts up to the thermostat. When the thermostat wants heat, it connects R to W; the 24 volts travels back down the W wire to a relay or the control board, which starts the heating sequence (Lesson 3). For cooling it connects R to Y, which closes the contactor in the outdoor unit, and for the fan, R to G.

The C, or common, wire completes the circuit back to the transformer without switching anything, which gives a smart thermostat steady power for its screen and Wi-Fi. Because the thermostat only switches 24-volt signals, small thin wires are enough.

Not every thermostat works this way. Electric baseboard heaters often use line-voltage thermostats that switch the 120- or 240-volt heater circuit directly, as the Department of Energy notes. Those are a different, more dangerous kind of wiring.

blocks.html: The letters are a common convention, but there are no standard wire colors, and brands differ, especially for heat pumps (O versus B). The equipment manufacturer’s instructions and wiring diagram are the final word.

A thermostat doesn’t switch on the instant the room drops a hair below the setting and off the instant it’s a hair above. It waits for a small difference, often called the differential or deadband, before it turns on, and it shuts off a little past the setting. Without that gap, the equipment would start and stop every few seconds. The widget shows the cycles: the room temperature drifts down, the heat comes on, the room warms past the setting, and the heat shuts off.

The Department of Energy says you can save as much as 10 percent a year on heating and cooling by turning your thermostat back 7 to 10°F (4 to 6 Celsius degrees) from its normal setting for 8 hours a day, for example while you sleep or are away. The savings are bigger in milder climates. DOE also corrects a common myth: a furnace doesn’t work harder to reheat the house than it saved, because a cooler house loses heat more slowly the whole time it’s set back.

Programmable thermostats make setback automatic, returning the house to normal before you wake or get home. DOE notes that ordinary setback isn’t recommended for heat pumps in heating mode unless the thermostat is designed for heat pumps (Lesson 6).

Smart thermostats add features that ENERGY STAR describes: they learn your preferences, can be controlled from a phone, use geofencing to know when you’re heading home, and report how your system runs. ENERGY STAR certified smart thermostats also drop into a low-power standby mode when idle. Make sure any thermostat you buy is compatible with your system.

A thermostat can only control what it senses. DOE says it should be on an interior wall, away from direct sunlight, drafts, doorways, skylights and windows, and that furniture shouldn’t sit in front of or below it, since that blocks natural air movement. A thermostat in the sun or above a lamp reads too warm and shuts the heat off early; one in a draft reads too cold.

  • If the thermostat calls but nothing happens, check the breaker once (Reset a Tripped Circuit Breaker); if it trips again, leave it off and call.

lessons.title: Efficiency, Sizing and the House
lessons.short: Heat loss through walls and ceilings, R-values, why oversized equipment short-cycles and leaves the air clammy, load calculations, and every efficiency rating side by side.
lessons.intro: The best system is sized for the house it serves, and the house comes first: insulation and air sealing shrink the load before any equipment is chosen. This lesson does the math.

blocks.html:
Heat conducts through every wall, ceiling, floor and window at a rate set by three things: the area, the temperature difference across it, and how well it resists heat flow. That resistance is the R-value. Physics books write it as the thickness divided by the material’s thermal conductivity; in the United States it’s quoted in ft²·°F·h/BTU, usually without the units. A 3.5-inch fiberglass batt in a wall is about R-11, and a 6.5-inch batt is about R-19.

Add up the losses through every surface, plus the heat carried out by air leaking through the house, and you have the house’s heating load. In summer the flows reverse and sunshine through windows and the heat from people and appliances add to the cooling load, which also has a latent part: the moisture the air conditioner must remove.

Q = A × ΔT ÷ R  (Q in BTU/h, A in ft², ΔT in °F, R in ft²·°F·h/BTU)
Example: 1,000 ft² of ceiling, 70°F inside and 20°F outside (ΔT = 50):
R-11 → 1,000 × 50 ÷ 11 ≈ 4,545 BTU/h (1,332 W); R-49 → 1,000 × 50 ÷ 49 ≈ 1,020 BTU/h (299 W)

blocks.cap: Heat flow through one flat layer at steady temperatures, Q = A·ΔT/R, ignoring framing, air leaks and sunshine. 1 BTU/h = 0.2931 W (NIST). The recommended attic levels are ENERGY STAR’s, based on the 2021 International Energy Conservation Code.

blocks.h: Why the first inches count most
blocks.html: Because heat flow goes as 1/R, each added layer saves less than the one before. Going from R-11 to R-19 in the example above cuts the loss by about 1,900 BTU/h; going from R-38 to R-49 cuts only about 300 more. That’s why an uninsulated or thinly insulated attic is often the best first project, and why the recommended level depends on the climate.

blocks.html:
An oversized air conditioner cools the air fast and shuts off before it has run long enough to pull much water out. The Department of Energy’s Building America program explains that an oversized system quickly meets the temperature setting, and the water sitting on the coil can evaporate back into the airstream when it stops. The result is a house that’s cool but clammy. ENERGY STAR adds that oversized equipment may cycle too often, giving less comfort and a shorter life, and a cold-climate guide hosted by DOE warns that grossly oversizing heat pumps leads to excessive cycling, low efficiency and poor summer dehumidification.

Old rules of thumb, so many square feet per ton, are based on older construction, and Building America notes that even new code-built homes would likely be oversized by them. The industry method is a room-by-room load calculation, usually ACCA’s Manual J, followed by Manual S to select equipment and Manual D to design the ducts. ENERGY STAR advises asking your contractor to size the system from your home’s actual characteristics: its size, insulation and windows, not a rule of thumb.

blocks.h: Installation counts as much as the label
blocks.html: ENERGY STAR says improper installation can reduce a system’s efficiency by up to 30 percent. A quality installation includes a load calculation, airflow set to the manufacturer’s specifications, a refrigerant charge that’s tested and adjusted, and ducts inspected and sealed. ENERGY STAR certified heat pumps and air conditioners can save up to 20 percent on heating and cooling costs, but only if they’re installed well.

The cheapest heating and cooling is the kind you don’t need. The Department of Energy says air sealing can save 10 to 20 percent on heating and cooling bills, and that combining an efficient system with insulation, air sealing and thermostat settings can cut those bills by about 30 percent. Sealing and insulating first also shrinks the load, so the new equipment can be smaller and cheaper.

Building and energy codes set minimum insulation and equipment requirements where you live, and they change over time. The local code and the authority having jurisdiction decide what applies to your house and what needs a permit and an inspection.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting by Symptom
lessons.short: A finder for the most common problems, and a calm order for thinking them through: safety, settings, power, airflow, then the equipment.
lessons.intro: Plenty of no-heat and no-cooling calls end with a simple fix: a thermostat setting, a tripped breaker or a clogged filter. Check those safely, learn which signs mean stop, and you’ll also be able to tell a technician exactly what you saw.

blocks.html:
1. Safety first. A sounding CO alarm or a smell of gas is an emergency, not a repair (see below). So is smoke or a burning electrical smell.
  2. Settings. Is the thermostat in the right mode (Heat or Cool), set past the room temperature, and powered? Is the fan on Auto or On?
  3. Power. Is a breaker tripped? Many furnaces and air handlers also have a service switch nearby, and outdoor units have a disconnect. Reset a tripped breaker once; if it trips again, leave it off and call (Reset a Tripped Circuit Breaker).
  4. Airflow. Is the filter clean? Are registers and return grilles open and clear? Is the outdoor unit free of leaves, snow and ice?
  5. Water and ice. Water around the indoor unit or ice on the coil or lines points to drainage or airflow problems, or to low refrigerant.
  6. Equipment. If all of that checks out, the problem is inside the equipment. Note what you saw and heard, any blinking fault light you can see, and when it started. That’s what a technician needs.

The finder covers common problems in typical home systems. Your equipment’s manual explains its own settings and any fault codes.

blocks.html:
If the CO alarm sounds: immediately move everyone outside to fresh air, call 911 or the fire department, and don’t go back in until emergency responders say it’s safe. Don’t try to find the source. Don’t use a malfunctioning appliance again until it has been serviced (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission).

If you smell gas (gas companies add an odorant that smells like rotten eggs so leaks can be noticed): treat it as an emergency and follow your gas utility’s emergency instructions right away. The utility and the fire department handle suspected gas leaks.

If you see smoke or flames, get out and call 911.

Good notes save time and money. Write down the date and time, what the thermostat said (mode, setting, room temperature), what ran and what didn’t (indoor blower, outdoor fan, burners), any noises or smells, whether a breaker had tripped, and any blinking light you could see without opening a panel. Many control boards blink a status light in a pattern; the furnace’s manual explains it. If you have your equipment’s model and serial numbers from the nameplate, have them handy.

quiz.q: The air conditioner isn’t cooling. Which should you check first?
opts: The thermostat mode and setting, the breaker, and the filter
quiz.why: Settings, power and airflow are safe owner checks; refrigerant and electrical tests are for technicians.

quiz.q: A breaker for the outdoor unit trips again right after you reset it. What now?
opts: Reset it again until it holds
Leave it off and call a qualified technician or electrician
Tape it in the on position
Swap it with a bigger breaker
quiz.why: A breaker that trips again is a warning. Leave it off and call.

quiz.q: Your CO alarm sounds. What comes first?
opts: Open windows and find the source
Move everyone outside to fresh air, then call 911 or the fire department
Turn the furnace off and back on
quiz.why: Outside first, then call. Don’t go back in until responders say it’s safe.

lessons.title: Maintenance and Doing Your Own Work
lessons.short: What owners can do (filters, the outdoor unit, the thermostat, breakers, vents and the condensate drain), the yearly professional checkup, what the law reserves for pros, and the skill ladder.
lessons.intro: Owners can do a lot to keep a system healthy, and none of it requires opening the equipment. This lesson lists those jobs, explains what a professional tune-up covers, and draws a clear line around the work that the law or plain safety reserves for licensed and certified pros.

blocks.html:
• Filters. Check monthly and change at least every three months, or as your system’s manufacturer recommends; more often with pets, dust or constant use (Change a Furnace Air Filter).
  • The outdoor unit. Keep leaves, grass clippings, snow and plants away from it, following the clearances in its manual. Don’t stack things on top: the fan blows up through it.
  • Vents outside. Keep the furnace’s vent and air-intake pipes, the dryer vent and other outlets clear of snow and debris, as the U.S. Fire Administration advises.
  • Registers and returns. Keep them open and unblocked, and vacuum the grilles.
  • The thermostat. Replace batteries if it uses them; review the schedule each season.
  • The condensate drain. Know where it ends and check that it drips in cooling season. EPA advises keeping drip pans clean and drain lines flowing; follow your manual for any drain care it recommends.
  • Alarms. Test CO and smoke alarms monthly (Test Smoke and CO Alarms).
  • Clearance. Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from heat sources (USFA), and keep the furnace area free of stored items.

ENERGY STAR suggests checking the cooling system in the spring and the heating system in the fall. Its checklist for a contractor’s visit includes:

  • Every system: checking thermostat settings, tightening electrical connections and measuring motor voltage and current, lubricating moving parts, inspecting the condensate drain, and checking that the controls start, run and shut down safely.
  • Cooling: cleaning the indoor and outdoor coils, checking and adjusting the refrigerant level, and cleaning and adjusting the blower to keep the airflow right.
  • Heating: checking gas (or oil) connections, gas pressure, burner combustion and the heat exchanger.

CPSC, CDC and the U.S. Fire Administration all advise a yearly professional inspection of fuel-burning heating equipment, including the chimney, flue and vents.

blocks.h: What needs a pro, and why
blocks.html:
• Refrigerant. Federal law: EPA Section 608 requires certification to attach gauges, add or remove refrigerant, or open the refrigerant circuit, and venting refrigerant is illegal. Refrigerant under pressure can also cause serious cold burns.
  • Gas. Gas piping, gas valves, burners, ignition and venting are where fires and carbon monoxide come from. Leave them to qualified technicians and your gas utility.
  • Electrical inside the equipment. Furnaces and air handlers run on 120 volts or more; outdoor units and electric heat on 240 volts. Their control boards, contactors and motors are a technician’s job.
  • Installing or replacing equipment. Sizing, ducts, refrigerant lines, gas, venting and wiring all come together. Many places require a permit and an inspection, and some states and localities require contractors to be licensed. ENERGY STAR suggests checking your state’s license and insurance requirements before you hire.

ENERGY STAR’s tips for hiring: check your state’s license and insurance requirements, ask for references and call them, expect the contractor to size the system from your home’s size, insulation and windows, ask them to inspect the ducts for leaks and insulation and to measure the airflow, and sign a written proposal with prices, model numbers, the schedule and the warranty before work starts. For refrigerant work, EPA suggests asking to see the technician’s Section 608 certification.

• Keep the manuals for your furnace, air handler, outdoor unit and thermostat together, with a log of filter changes and service visits.
  • Turn off power at the equipment’s switch or breaker before you do anything near moving parts, such as cleaning around the outdoor unit.
  • Work with a helper the first time you try anything new.

• If doing a job would mean removing a panel the manual reserves for a technician, stop there.
  • Never bypass a safety switch, run a furnace with its doors off, or add refrigerant from a store-bought can to a home system.
  • Any CO alarm, gas smell, burning smell or water near electrical parts: follow the emergency steps in Lesson 11.

quiz.q: How often does ENERGY STAR say to check your HVAC filter?
opts: Every month, changing it at least every three months
quiz.why: Check monthly, change at least every three months, more often if it looks dirty.

quiz.q: Which job requires EPA Section 608 certification?
opts: Clearing leaves from the outdoor unit
quiz.why: Any work that opens the refrigerant circuit, including attaching gauges, requires certification.

quiz.q: When does ENERGY STAR suggest scheduling checkups?
opts: Cooling in the spring, heating in the fall
quiz.why: Pre-season: cooling in spring, heating in fall.

quiz.q: Before hiring an HVAC contractor, ENERGY STAR suggests you:
opts: Check your state’s license and insurance requirements and call references
quiz.why: Licensing, insurance, references, a proper sizing calculation and a written proposal.

lessons.title: Careers in HVAC
lessons.short: What HVACR technicians do, pay and job outlook from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, training programs and apprenticeships, EPA certification and state licenses.
lessons.intro: Every building needs heating, cooling and clean air, and the people who install and fix those systems are in demand. Here’s what the work is like, what it pays, and how people get started.

blocks.html:
The Bureau of Labor Statistics calls them heating, air conditioning and refrigeration mechanics and installers, and most people say HVACR technicians. They install, maintain and repair heating, cooling, ventilation and refrigeration systems; install electrical parts and wiring; inspect and test systems; talk with customers about problems; replace worn parts; recommend maintenance; and keep records of their work.

Some specialize: in radiant heating, in testing and balancing, or in commercial refrigeration for grocery stores, hotels and restaurants. Some focus on installing new systems, others on service and repair. About two-thirds work for plumbing, heating and air-conditioning contractors.

BLS reports a median pay of $61,010 a year in May 2025, or $29.33 an hour, meaning half earned more and half less. There were 440,900 jobs in 2025, and employment is projected to grow 11 percent from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the average for all occupations. That’s about 40,600 openings a year, many of them to replace workers who retire or change careers.

BLS expects growth from new commercial buildings, including data centers, and new homes, and from more advanced climate-control systems. Because so much of the work is repair and replacement, technicians are also needed to retrofit, upgrade and replace existing systems.

Most HVACR technicians complete a program at a technical or trade school or community college, lasting from 6 months to 2 years and leading to a certificate or an associate’s degree. Some employers hire high school graduates and train them; BLS suggests that high school students take vocational education, math and physics. New technicians start with basic tasks and move to harder ones, and the job involves a lengthy period of on-the-job training.

Others train through apprenticeships, which usually last several years and combine paid on-the-job training with technical instruction each year. A registered apprenticeship, approved through the U.S. Department of Labor, gives you paid work experience with a mentor, wage increases as your skills grow, classroom instruction and a portable, nationally recognized credential. Search for openings at Apprenticeship.gov.

blocks.html:
EPA certification. BLS notes that EPA requires nearly all HVAC technicians to be certified in proper refrigerant handling. Under Section 608, there are four types: Type I for small appliances, Type II for high- and very-high-pressure equipment such as home air conditioners and heat pumps, Type III for low-pressure equipment, and Universal for all three. Technicians pass an EPA-approved test given by an EPA-approved certifying organization, often as part of a school program, and the certification doesn’t expire.

State and local licenses. Some states and localities require HVAC technicians or contractors to be licensed, so check the rules where you plan to work. Many manufacturers and industry groups offer further certifications; most are optional, though some employers prefer or require them. A driver’s license is often needed to get to job sites.

Technicians work in homes, schools, hospitals, offices and factories, often in cramped attics and crawlspaces and sometimes outdoors in any weather. BLS reports that HVAC technicians have one of the highest rates of injuries and illnesses of all occupations, from hazards such as burns from electrical parts or chemicals and muscle strains from moving heavy equipment; they wear protective gear when working with refrigerants. Most work full time, and many are on call for emergencies or work overtime during the peak heating and cooling seasons.

BLS lists the important qualities: customer-service skills, attention to detail, math, mechanical skills, physical stamina and strength, problem-solving and technology skills. The physics in this course, from latent heat to the Carnot limit, is the same physics technicians use every day.
Pay and job figures are from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook, page last modified August 27, 2026. Pay varies by location, experience and specialty.
