finder.name: No heat
finder.q: What’s happening when the heat should be on?

opts.label: Nothing runs at all: no fan, no sound
causes: The thermostat is off, set to Cool, set below the room temperature, or its batteries are dead
A tripped breaker, or the furnace’s service switch turned off
A furnace door panel not fully closed (many furnaces have a door safety switch)
A failed control part, such as the transformer or control board
checks: Set the thermostat to Heat and a few degrees above the room temperature; replace its batteries if it uses them.
Check the breaker for the furnace or air handler (Being an Adult 101 has a guide), and the service switch near the unit.
Make sure the furnace’s front panels are seated as they were.
opts.stop: If the breaker trips again right after you reset it, leave it off and call.
opts.pro: If it has power and the thermostat is calling but nothing happens, a technician can test the control circuit.

opts.label: The fan blows, but the air isn’t warm (gas furnace)
causes: The thermostat fan is set to On, so it blows between heating cycles
The burners aren’t lighting, or they shut off on a safety: a pressure switch, the flame sensor or the high-limit switch
A clogged filter making the high-limit switch trip
The gas supply is off
checks: Set the thermostat fan to Auto.
Check and change the filter.
Note any blinking status light you can see without opening the furnace; the manual explains the pattern.
Check that the outdoor vent and intake pipes aren’t blocked by snow or debris.
opts.stop: Don’t keep resetting a furnace that keeps shutting off, and never bypass a safety switch.
opts.pro: Ignition, flame-sensor, venting and gas-valve problems are for a qualified technician.

opts.label: Heat pump: it runs and runs, or the air feels only lukewarm
causes: Very cold weather: a heat pump’s capacity and efficiency drop as it gets colder, so it runs longer
A defrost cycle in progress
A dirty filter or blocked outdoor unit
Low refrigerant or a failed part
checks: Make sure the thermostat is on Heat, not Cool.
Check the filter.
Clear snow, ice and leaves away from the outdoor unit.
See whether the thermostat shows auxiliary or emergency heat running all the time.
opts.stop: If the outdoor coil stays solid with ice for hours, turn the system to emergency heat if your thermostat has it, and call.
opts.pro: Defrost controls, refrigerant and the reversing valve are technician work; refrigerant work needs EPA certification.

finder.name: No cooling
finder.q: What do you see at the outdoor unit?

opts.label: The outdoor unit is silent and its fan isn’t turning
causes: The thermostat isn’t set to Cool, or is set above the room temperature
A tripped breaker for the outdoor unit (it usually has its own), or its outdoor disconnect switched off
A failed contactor, capacitor or fan motor
Some systems shut the cooling off when the condensate pan fills, to prevent a water leak
checks: Set the thermostat to Cool, several degrees below the room temperature.
Check the breakers for the outdoor unit and the furnace or air handler.
Look for water around the indoor unit or a full condensate pump.
opts.stop: If a breaker trips again, leave it off. Don’t open the outdoor unit’s electrical panel.
opts.pro: Contactors, capacitors and motors are tested and replaced by technicians.

opts.label: The outdoor unit hums, but its fan doesn’t spin
causes: A failed capacitor or fan motor
A seized or overheated compressor or fan
checks: Turn the cooling off at the thermostat to protect the compressor.
opts.stop: Turn the cooling off and leave it off until it’s repaired. Don’t poke anything into the fan.
opts.pro: A technician needs to test the motor-starting parts and the compressor.

opts.label: Everything runs, but the air from the vents isn’t cold
causes: A dirty filter or indoor coil cutting the airflow
A dirty outdoor coil that can’t shed heat
Low refrigerant from a leak
A compressor problem
checks: Change the filter.
Look at the outdoor coil: clear leaves, cottonwood fluff and grass clippings from around it.
Check for ice on the copper lines or the indoor unit.
opts.stop: If you find ice, turn the cooling off and let it melt before running it again.
opts.pro: Low refrigerant means a leak. EPA advises having it found and repaired, not just topped off, by a Section 608 certified technician.

finder.name: Short cycling
finder.q: What does the cycling look like?

opts.label: It turns on and off every few minutes
causes: A thermostat in a bad spot: in sunlight, near a lamp, or near a supply register
A dirty filter making a safety switch trip
Oversized equipment
A refrigerant or control problem
checks: Look at where the thermostat is: DOE says an interior wall, away from sun, drafts, doors and windows.
Change the filter.
Note how long each run lasts and how often it starts.
opts.stop: Not dangerous by itself, but it wastes energy and wears out parts.
opts.pro: A technician can check the safeties, the refrigerant charge and whether the system is oversized.

opts.label: Furnace burners light, go out within seconds, and try again
causes: The flame sensor isn’t detecting the flame (often a dirty sensor)
A venting or pressure-switch problem
checks: Note any blinking status light pattern you can see.
Make sure the outdoor vent and intake pipes are clear.
Make sure your CO alarms work.
opts.stop: Don’t keep resetting it. If a CO alarm sounds, follow the CO steps.
opts.pro: Flame sensors, ignition and venting are serviced by a qualified technician.

finder.name: Ice on the coil or lines
finder.q: Where is the ice, and when?

opts.label: On the copper lines or indoor unit, in cooling mode
causes: Low airflow: a dirty filter, blocked return grilles or closed registers, or a weak blower
Low refrigerant from a leak
A dirty indoor coil
checks: Switch the thermostat from Cool to Off so the ice can melt, and put down towels for the meltwater.
Change the filter, and open every register and return grille.
After it has fully thawed, run it again and watch.
opts.stop: Don’t chip or scrape ice off the coil or lines.
opts.pro: If it ices again with a clean filter and open vents, have a Section 608 certified technician check the refrigerant and the coil.

opts.label: On a heat pump’s outdoor unit in winter
causes: Light frost is normal; the defrost cycle melts it
Heavy ice that stays can mean a defrost-control or sensor problem, low refrigerant, or water dripping on it from a gutter
Snow drifting against the unit
checks: Keep snow cleared away from the sides and top.
Look for a gutter or roof edge dripping onto it.
opts.stop: Don’t chip ice off the coil; the fins and tubes bend and puncture easily.
opts.pro: Ice that stays for hours needs a technician.

finder.name: Water around the indoor unit
finder.q: When does the water show up?

opts.label: During cooling (air conditioner or heat pump)
causes: A clogged condensate drain line
A cracked or rusted drain pan
A failed condensate pump
A frozen coil melting
A drain line that has come apart
checks: Turn the cooling off to stop making water.
Find where the drain line ends and see if it’s dripping or blocked.
Look for a disconnected drain hose or a condensate pump that isn’t running.
Dry the area quickly; EPA says to act fast on moisture to prevent mold.
opts.stop: If water is near outlets, cords or the equipment’s wiring, don’t touch it; turn the system off at the thermostat and call.
opts.pro: Pans, pumps and drains inside the unit are serviced by a technician.

opts.label: During heating, with a high-efficiency furnace
causes: A condensing furnace’s condensate drain, trap or pump is blocked or leaking
A disconnected drain hose
checks: See whether a drain hose has visibly come loose or the condensate pump isn’t running.
opts.stop: Don’t open the furnace. The condensate is acidic; wipe it up and keep pets away.
opts.pro: Condensate traps and drains inside the furnace are a technician’s job.

finder.name: Weak airflow
finder.q: Is it weak at every register, or just some?

opts.label: Weak everywhere
causes: A dirty filter
Blocked return grilles
A dirty indoor coil or blower wheel
An iced-over coil in cooling mode
A blower motor problem
checks: Change the filter.
Clear furniture, rugs and curtains from return grilles.
Look for ice on the indoor unit or lines.
opts.stop: If you hear squealing or grinding, turn the system off.
opts.pro: Blower and coil cleaning, and motor problems, are technician work.

opts.label: Weak in one or two rooms
causes: A closed or blocked register
A crushed, kinked or disconnected duct
A damper partly closed
Leaky ducts losing air before it arrives
checks: Open the registers fully and clear furniture away.
Look at the ducts you can reach in a basement or attic for kinks and loose joints.
opts.stop: Not urgent.
opts.pro: A contractor can test the ducts for leaks, balance the airflow, or add a return path.

finder.name: Some rooms too hot or cold

opts.label: Upstairs or far rooms too hot in summer or cold in winter
causes: Leaky or undersized ducts to those rooms
Little insulation or many air leaks in that part of the house
Sun pouring through windows
No easy return path from those rooms
checks: Open the registers fully.
Close blinds on sunny summer afternoons.
Check the attic insulation against ENERGY STAR’s recommended levels.
opts.stop: Not urgent.
opts.pro: Duct testing and sealing, balancing, added returns, zoning, or a ductless unit for a problem room.

opts.label: One radiator or baseboard stays cold (hot-water heat)
causes: Air trapped in the radiator or loop
A closed valve on that radiator
A circulator or zone-valve problem
checks: Make sure the radiator’s valve is open.
DOE suggests eliminating trapped air from hot-water radiators once or twice a season; follow your boiler manual, or ask a technician to show you.
opts.stop: Radiator water can be hot enough to scald. Don’t touch the boiler’s controls or relief valve.
opts.pro: Pumps, zone valves and boiler controls are technician work.

opts.label: Rotten eggs, or like gas
causes: A possible natural gas or propane leak. Gas companies add an odorant that smells like rotten eggs so leaks can be noticed.
checks: Treat it as an emergency and follow your gas utility’s emergency instructions right away.
opts.stop: Now. A gas smell is an emergency for the gas utility and the fire department, not a repair job.
opts.pro: Your gas utility first. After it’s safe, a qualified technician repairs the leak.

opts.label: Exhaust or fumes when the furnace runs
causes: A venting problem: DOE says that if you smell exhaust gases, you have a venting problem that could affect your health
A blocked or disconnected vent pipe, or a damaged heat exchanger
checks: Make sure your CO alarms are working.
Check that the outdoor vent isn’t blocked by snow or debris.
opts.stop: Stop using the furnace until it’s checked. If a CO alarm sounds, get everyone outside and call 911.
opts.pro: A qualified technician should inspect the venting and heat exchanger before you use it again.

opts.label: Burning plastic or electrical smell, or smoke
causes: An overheating motor or wiring
checks: Turn the system off at the thermostat.
opts.stop: If you see smoke or flames, get out and call 911.
opts.pro: Have it inspected before running it again.

opts.label: Musty or moldy
causes: Standing water in a drain pan or a clogged condensate drain
Mold in the ducts, on the coil or elsewhere from too much moisture
Indoor humidity above 60 percent
checks: Measure the humidity with a hygrometer: EPA suggests 30 to 50 percent.
Check that the condensate drain is flowing.
Run bath and kitchen fans that vent outdoors.
opts.stop: If you suspect the system itself is contaminated with mold, EPA advises not running it until it’s cleaned.
opts.pro: Coil, pan and duct cleaning, and finding the moisture source.

finder.name: CO alarm
finder.q: Is it a full alarm, or a short chirp?

opts.label: A full alarm
causes: A fuel-burning appliance, such as a furnace, boiler or water heater, that isn’t working or isn’t vented properly
A vehicle or generator running in or near the home
checks: Immediately move outside to fresh air.
Call your emergency services, the fire department or 911.
Do a head count to check that everyone is out.
Don’t go back in until the emergency responders give you permission. Don’t try to find the source.
opts.stop: Now. Never ignore a CO alarm (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission).
opts.pro: If an appliance was the source, don’t use it again until trained personnel have serviced it.

opts.label: A short chirp every so often
causes: A low battery
The alarm signaling the end of its life
checks: Follow the alarm’s instructions to tell a low-battery chirp from an end-of-life signal.
Replace the battery, or the whole alarm if it’s at the end of its life (Being an Adult 101 has a guide).
opts.stop: Don’t leave the home unprotected: replace it promptly.
opts.pro: None needed for a battery-powered alarm; hardwired alarms are an electrician’s job.

opts.label: A bang or boom when the furnace lights
causes: Gas lighting late, after some has built up (delayed ignition), often from dirty burners or an ignition problem
checks: Turn the heat off at the thermostat.
opts.stop: Don’t keep running it. Have it checked before using the heat again.
opts.pro: Burners, ignition and gas pressure are a qualified technician’s job.

opts.label: Squealing, grinding or scraping
causes: Worn blower or fan motor bearings
A loose or damaged blower wheel or fan blade
Something caught in a fan
checks: Turn the system off at the thermostat.
Look (without reaching in) for sticks or debris on top of the outdoor unit.
opts.stop: Turn it off to avoid more damage. Keep hands out of fans.
opts.pro: Motors and fans are replaced by technicians.

opts.label: Clicking that repeats, but the system never starts
causes: An ignition problem in a furnace
A relay or control problem
checks: Check the thermostat settings and batteries.
Note any status light pattern.
opts.stop: If you smell gas, follow the gas-smell guidance instead.
opts.pro: Ignition and control diagnosis.

opts.label: Hissing or bubbling near the refrigerant lines
causes: Possibly a refrigerant leak
checks: Note where the sound comes from and whether cooling is weak.
opts.stop: Don’t touch the lines or try to seal them.
opts.pro: Refrigerant leaks are found and repaired by a Section 608 certified technician.

opts.label: They’ve crept up over the years
causes: Aging equipment: ENERGY STAR suggests a professional evaluation for heat pumps and air conditioners over 10 years old and furnaces or boilers over 15
Dirty filters and coils
Leaky ducts
Missing insulation and air leaks
checks: Change the filter.
Program a thermostat setback.
Look at the attic insulation and accessible ducts.
opts.stop: Not urgent.
opts.pro: A tune-up, a duct leakage test or a home energy assessment.

opts.label: A sudden jump
causes: A heat pump running on backup electric heat
A system running constantly because of low refrigerant, a stuck relay or a blocked coil
Thermostat settings that changed
checks: Check the thermostat’s mode, schedule and any “aux heat” indicator.
Check the filter and the outdoor unit.
opts.stop: Not dangerous, but costly.
opts.pro: A technician can find out why it’s running so much.

Install a window air conditioner, following its instructions

Air-seal and add attic insulation

Straighten bent coil fins with a fin comb
